# 17 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization

Determinants do more than solve linear systems: their expansion is a signed sum
over permutations, hence over directed cycle covers.  Choosing matrix entries
carefully makes unwanted covers cancel, leaving spanning trees, matchings, or
parity structures.  Random evaluation then turns a symbolic nonzeroness
question into finite-field linear algebra.

There are two levels to keep separate throughout this chapter.  A polynomial
identity is exact: if a determinant polynomial is nonzero, the desired graph
object exists.  A random field substitution is only a fast test for that fact:
a nonzero evaluated value is a witness, while a zero can be unlucky.

## 1. Pfaffians and hafnians

For an even-dimensional **skew-symmetric** matrix $A$ ($A^T=-A$ and diagonal
zero), the Pfaffian is the pairing analogue of a determinant: it sums signed
products over perfect pairings.  For the $2\times2$ matrix
$\begin{pmatrix}0&a\\-a&0\end{pmatrix}$, the Pfaffian is $a$ and its determinant
is $a^2$.  In general it satisfies

$$\operatorname{Pf}(A)^{2}=\det A.$$

The identity explains why Pfaffian algorithms can recognize certain weighted
matching structures with determinant-like cost.  Eliminate pairs of rows and
columns together.  If pivot `A[i][j]` is used, swap indices into the active
pair, account for the Pfaffian sign, multiply the pivot, and apply the
skew-symmetric Schur-complement update.  This is $O(n^3)$ over a field of
characteristic not two.  The hafnian removes signs and directly counts weighted
perfect pairings, but its general algorithms are exponential; do not confuse a
Pfaffian with a general perfect-matching counter.

## 2. Tutte matrix

For an undirected graph, put an independent indeterminate $x_{ij}$ above the
diagonal, $-x_{ij}$ below it, and zero on nonedges.  This is its **Tutte
matrix**.  The central theorem says its determinant is a nonzero polynomial if
and only if the graph has a perfect matching.  One direction is intuitive from
the determinant expansion: a surviving cycle cover supplies alternating edges,
hence a matching; a perfect matching supplies a distinct monomial.

Substitute independent uniform field values from a set $S$ and compute one
determinant.  A nonzero result certifies a perfect matching.  If a perfect
matching exists, an $n$-vertex graph gives a false negative with probability at
most $n/|S|$ per trial.  Likewise, the evaluated rank is at most twice the
maximum matching size and equals it with high probability.  The symbolic
theorem is valid in characteristic two as well, but sampling only from
$\mathbb F_2$ gives a useless error bound; use a sufficiently large field or
extension field.

## 3. Schwartz–Zippel and PIT

A nonzero polynomial of total degree $d$ evaluated independently and uniformly
over a finite set $S$ vanishes with probability at most $d/|S|$ (the
Schwartz--Zippel lemma).  Record all three quantities: degree, field size, and
number of trials.  With $t$ independent trials, the bound becomes
$(d/|S|)^t$.  Random evaluation can produce a false zero but never a false
symbolic witness.  Use fresh randomness, avoid tiny fields, and repeat when the
error budget is not negligible.

## 4. Determinant polynomials and updates

$det(A+xB)$ packages a family of rank/determinant questions into one polynomial;
evaluate at enough field points and interpolate.  The matrix determinant lemma
and Sherman–Morrison give rank-one updates when the required inverse exists.
The adjugate identity

$$A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)I$$

remains meaningful when $A$ is singular and is often the safer symbolic object.

## A safe randomized workflow

1. Define the symbolic matrix and prove which graph property makes its target
   polynomial nonzero.
2. Bound the total degree of that polynomial and choose a field much larger
   than the degree times the desired error margin.
3. Sample every independent entry freshly, evaluate, and run ordinary field
   elimination.
4. State the one-sided conclusion precisely: a nonzero answer is certain; a
   zero answer is “probably absent” with the computed error bound.

## Ordered practice

1. **Capstone — [Degree Harmony, ABC412 G](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc412/tasks/abc412_g?lang=en).** Weighted matching through determinant polynomials.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>Reduce the degree constraints to a minimum-weight perfect matching; encode weights as powers of a new variable and recover the lowest nonzero degree.</details>
2. **Alternate-method lab — [No Need, ABC056 D](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc056/tasks/arc070_b?lang=en).** Polynomial fingerprints.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>Card $i$ is necessary exactly when a subset of the other cards has sum in $[K-a_i,K)$. Replace each factor by $1+r_jx^{a_j}$, multiply modulo $x^K$, and divide by $1+r_ix^{a_i}$ to exclude card $i$. Distinct subsets give distinct square-free monomials in the formal variables $r_j$, so the relevant coefficient polynomial cannot cancel identically. Independent uniform substitutions in $\mathbb F_P$ turn this into a Monte Carlo test; bound the error over all tested coefficients with Schwartz–Zippel and a union bound (the official analysis obtains $O(N^2/P)$).</details>
